opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think three-dimensional intuition is mostly wrong, and the trick is knowing *when* it's wrong.

The picture everyone has in their head is a little 2D or 3D plot: there's a decision boundary, a point sitting on one side, and you nudge it across. That picture is useful for one thing. It reminds you that an attack is an optimization problem: you're walking along some surface trying to find a direction that changes the output. If you've forgotten that, the cartoon brings you back.

But almost every quantitative instinct you get from it is misleading. In three dimensions, if I tell you a point is close to a boundary, you imagine it's close in one particular direction, and most random directions don't get you there. In a hundred-thousand-dimensional input space, it's the reverse. There are so many directions that some tiny perturbation along a cleverly chosen one moves you a long way in the output, even though every individual coordinate barely changes. Small L-infinity balls are enormous in high dimensions. That fact is the whole reason adversarial examples exist, and your 3D brain will tell you it shouldn't work.

So the way I use it in practice is this. I'll sketch the low-dimensional picture to form a hypothesis. Something like, "this defense is probably creating a flat region in the loss so gradients vanish." Then I immediately stop trusting the picture and go measure. Do the gradients actually look like noise? Does the attack succeed if I swap in a smooth approximation of the non-differentiable component? Does loss go down as I increase iterations, or does it plateau suspiciously? Those checks are the things that actually break defenses, and they don't depend on whether my mental image was right.

The other place I've found the intuition actively harmful is with defenses whose authors drew the picture and stopped there. You see a figure of a nice clean margin around the data manifold and an argument that the attacker can't get through it. That figure is convincing because it's two-dimensional. The attacker doesn't live in two dimensions. A lot of what I've done is just taking those arguments seriously enough to ask, "Okay, but what happens in the other 99,998 directions?"

So my answer is that it's a good way to generate ideas and a terrible way to evaluate them. Use it to decide what to try, and then let the experiment tell you whether you were right.

r001.rationale: The response says 3D intuition is misleading for quantitative judgments in high-dimensional input spaces and describes how it can lead defense authors astray.

r002.rationale: It discusses many directions and small perturbations in high dimensions, but does not say that almost all points are close to a hyperplane.

r003.rationale: The response recommends testing whether a geometric hypothesis is right, but does not clearly state that attackers can learn which intuitions fail without understanding why.

r004.rationale: It treats a defense’s convincing 2D margin picture as a reason to investigate what happens in the many other dimensions.

fable-5.1.text:
I'd say it's mostly useless, and that's actually one of the more important things to internalize if you want to do this kind of work well.

The picture everyone has in their head when they first hear about adversarial examples is a two-dimensional one. You've got a decision boundary, it's some curve, there's a data point sitting near it, and you nudge the point across. That's a fine picture for explaining the idea at a dinner party. But almost every intuition you'd derive from that picture turns out to be wrong in a few thousand dimensions. Things like how much volume is near the boundary, how far a "typical" point is from the nearest adversarial point, what a random direction does versus the gradient direction. In high dimensions almost all the volume of a ball is at the surface. Random directions are almost always nearly orthogonal to each other. A perturbation that's tiny per pixel is enormous in L2. None of that matches anything you can draw.

So in practice I try to replace visual intuition with two other things. One is just math, honestly fairly simple math, doing the calculation rather than picturing it. The other, and this is the one I lean on most, is running the experiment. If I think a defense works because of some geometric story, I don't trust the story. I write the attack and see whether it breaks. The number of times a very plausible-sounding geometric argument has evaporated the moment someone actually ran a proper attack is, I think, most of the history of this field.

Where three-dimensional intuition does earn its keep is as a hypothesis generator. It's good for asking "what if the boundary is doing something like this" and then that gives you an experiment to run. The failure mode is treating it as evidence. A lot of broken defenses were published by very smart people who had a convincing picture in their heads, and the picture was doing the work that an evaluation should have been doing. So my rule is roughly: use the picture to decide what to try, never use it to decide what's true.

r001.rationale: The response says intuitions from a two-dimensional picture become wrong in high dimensions and warns that relying on such pictures can lead to broken defenses.

r002.rationale: It says most of a ball’s volume lies at its surface, but does not state that almost all points are near a hyperplane.

r003.rationale: It recommends running attacks to test geometric claims, but does not say attackers can learn which intuitions fail without understanding why.

r004.rationale: It describes geometric intuition as a hypothesis generator and cautions against treating it as evidence, but does not identify a defense’s reliance on failed intuition as a clue to where to investigate for weakness.

astra-6.text:
I find it useful for coming up with hypotheses, but I’m very suspicious of it as evidence. You draw a picture in two or three dimensions, and it looks like the defense has put this nice barrier between your input and the decision boundary. But the actual input has thousands or hundreds of thousands of coordinates. There may be a direction you can move that your picture just doesn’t capture.

So I’ll use the picture to ask, “What do I think this defense is doing? Why might this attack fail?” And then I want to turn that intuition into something I can test. Is the defense actually making it harder to find an adversarial example, or is it just making the gradient unhelpful to the particular optimizer I’m using? Those can look very similar in an experiment, but they’re very different claims.

The useful part of visual intuition is that it gives you a place to start. The dangerous part is when you let the picture convince you that you’ve ruled out all the other ways an attack could work.

r003.rationale: The response recommends testing hypotheses, but does not state that attackers can learn which geometric intuitions fail without understanding why.

r004.rationale: It warns that a defense may have weaknesses missed by a picture, but does not identify a defense relying on a failed geometric intuition as a clue for where to investigate.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s useful for generating hypotheses, but it’s very easy to fool yourself. You draw a picture in two or three dimensions, and you say, “Well, clearly the attack has to go around this obstacle.” But in a high-dimensional space, there may be lots of directions that your picture just doesn’t capture.

So I’ll use that intuition to come up with an attack, but then I want to test it. Does the optimization actually behave the way I expected? If it fails, is that because the defense is robust, or because I’ve chosen a bad way to search? That distinction is really important. An attack failing tells you something about that attack; it doesn’t, by itself, tell you that there isn’t an adversarial example.
